HEALTH CRISIS: DRC EBOLA OUTBREAK

DR Congo — Ebola Outbreak

Ebola Outbreak Is Now the Second-Deadliest Ever, and in Record Time

Second-deadliest outbreak on record. Health workers in protective gear respond to the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, which has killed 1,521 people across five provinces as of late July 2026.

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has already become the second-worst on record, and it is spreading much faster than previous outbreaks, the nation’s health ministry reported on Thursday. The official death toll has jumped to 1,521 people in fewer than three months.

Put another way, the species of Ebola behind the current outbreak, Bundibugyo, has killed more than five times as many people as previous outbreaks did in the same amount of time, officials from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said at a press briefing on Thursday. The last outbreak, which began in 2018 and was declared over in 2020, took more than 10 months to reach the same death toll.

… The virus ripping through eastern Congo is on pace to surpass the number of infections and deaths of the 2014-2016 Ebola crisis in West Africa, the worst outbreak ever that killed more than 11,000 people.

Source: NYTimes

DR Congo — Africa CDC

Africa CDC warns DRC Ebola outbreak fastest-growing ever recorded

Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya told an online briefing Thursday evening that the Ebola outbreak in DRC is “the fastest-growing ever recorded” and now the second-largest by total cases. Latest data shows 3,442 confirmed cases and 1,521 deaths, a fatality rate exceeding 44 per cent across 48 health zones in five provinces.

Critical constraints include limited contact tracing, climbing community cases, inadequate bed capacity, funding shortages, insecurity, unsafe burials, and infections among healthcare workers. Uganda’s success in containing the outbreak, with only 20 cases and two deaths, was praised as demonstrating effective political leadership and community engagement. Eleven other African countries are designated high-risk. Clinical trials for therapeutics targeting the Bundibugyo strain launched, significant given no licensed vaccines exist for this variant.

Source: Xinhua, 31 July 2026

Kenya — Ebola Response

Ebola quarantine center for Americans is up and working in Kenya despite a court ban

Despite local protests and High Court orders, Samaritan’s Purse confirmed seven US staff began a 21-day quarantine there in mid-July. The organization did not say where in Kenya their workers were quarantined but local media have reported that military tents in Laikipia Air Base would house the U.S.-backed Ebola facility. The air base is about 185 kilometers (115 miles) north from Nairobi, Kenya’s capital, near the town of Nanyuki.

Residents of Nanyuki have staged a series of protests against the facility recently, and three people died when the protests turned violent. Both Kenya’s Ministry of Health and the U.S. State Department did not respond to requests for comment about whether Americans were being quarantined in Kenya. A Kenyan court last month issued an order that barred the operationalization of the facility and Health Minister Aden Duale later ordered suspension of its construction.

Source: AP

Uganda — Ebola Response

Uganda succeeds in containing Ebola while DRC outbreak worsens

Uganda’s health ministry said advances in epidemiological investigations provided sufficient evidence transmission had been interrupted, declaring the outbreak over despite only 20 cases and two deaths recorded. Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi described a “moment of joy” as the last patient was released two weeks ago.

The facility at Mulago hospital, used during a 2025 outbreak, held leftover supplies and an emergency team on standby, allowing readiness within one day, Dr David Kaggwa said. Fifteen of the 20 positive cases came from DRC. Uganda closed its border despite the economic impact and quarantined over 6,000 contacts.

Source: BBC

DR Congo — Humanitarian Response

WFP appeals for $76 million as Ebola epidemic becomes DRC’s largest on record

The UN World Food Programme issued an urgent appeal on Friday for $101 million over six months to support the Ebola response in the Great Lakes region, with $76 million earmarked specifically for operations inside the Democratic Republic of Congo. WFP said speed of execution and lack of resources were the principal obstacles to containing the outbreak, now affecting five provinces — Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Tshopo and Haut-Uele — two months after being declared.

Of the total, $50 million is needed for immediate food and nutritional assistance, including hot meals and support for quarantined households. WFP separately said it requires $293.6 million over six months to sustain all of its DRC operations.

Source: UN

DRC: SECURITY & ECONOMY

DR Congo — Security

Congo’s Deal with Rwandan Genocidaire Group to Disarm

The Congolese government says it has secured an agreement with the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), a rebel grouping comprised of Rwandan genocidaires Interahamwe, to disarm, demobilize and, ultimately, move into cantonement. The deal, if implemented, would be presented as a significant breakthrough in a long-standing security issue that has poisoned relations between the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda for decades.

… At a press conference by Regional Integration Minister Floribert Anzuluni and Government Spokesperson Patrick Muyaya, Kinshasa said the agreement represents its share of commitments under the Washington Accords signed in 2025. Under the Washington agreements and the Concept of Operations (Conops), two mechanisms had been agreed on to address the FDLR issue: An initial awareness-raising phase aimed at securing the group’s voluntary surrender, followed, if necessary, by military neutralization.

Source: The East African

DR Congo — Economy

Copper Output Falls in July

Congo’s Mining Ministry reported copper output fell 12% year-on-year in July, citing power shortages and transport bottlenecks. The decline threatens government revenue, with copper accounting for 40% of exports. Chinese-owned Tenke Fungurume mine reported “severe disruptions.” Analysts warn prolonged shortages could undermine Kinshasa’s fiscal plans.

Source: Reuters

CONFLICT WATCH: ETHIOPIA

Ethiopia — Security

Ethiopian army and TPLF forces clash near Sudan border, raising fears of new war

Fighting broke out Saturday morning between the Ethiopian National Defense Force and Tigray People’s Liberation Front fighters near the village of Shererina in western Tigray, close to the Sudanese border, a senior TPLF official told AFP. Amanuel Assefa, a TPLF spokesman, said federal forces launched the attack and that combat, involving heavy artillery, was continuing into the day.

The clash occurred in a disputed area administered by Amhara nationalists and involved a TPLF unit known locally as “Army 70,” reportedly based across the border in Sudan. Federal and Tigrayan forces have been massed along the regional border for months, each accusing the other of seeking to trigger renewed conflict. The 2020-2022 Tigray war killed an estimated 600,000 people; the US ambassador and African Union Horn of Africa envoy Olusegun Obasanjo have both recently visited the region to seek mediation.

Source: AFP

Ethiopia — Oromia-Sidama

Oromia–Sidama Clashes Kill 22

Between 26–29 July, clashes along the Oromia–Sidama border left 22 dead and displaced thousands. Local officials confirmed the violence stemmed from land disputes. The latest fighting that erupted last week continued from Sunday through Wednesday, causing extensive casualties, destruction of homes and public infrastructure, and renewed displacement.

Residents said the latest violence has also devastated livelihoods. Thousands of people displaced during last month’s clashes had returned hoping to harvest mature crops, including maize, teff, and beans, only to be forced to flee again. The unrest highlights Ethiopia’s fragile inter-ethnic relations.

Source: Addis Standard

Ethiopia — Saudi Arabia

Saudi Arabia Executes 5 Ethiopians over Drug-related Charges, Rights Group Says

Five Ethiopians were executed in Saudi Arabia this week on drug-related charges following a trial that allegedly did not follow due process and lasted a few minutes without a translator, according to Human Rights Watch. The rights organization said Tuesday at least 79 other Ethiopians remain at imminent risk of execution on similar charges.

It cited the European Saudi Organization for Human Rights, which said at least 116 people have been executed this year. Human Rights Watch said the five were charged with possessing hashish, a type of cannabis.

Source: AP

Ethiopia — GERD

GERD Fourth Filling Confirmed

Ethiopia’s Water Minister Habtamu Itefa confirmed the fourth filling of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam reservoir was completed. The announcement reignited tensions with Egypt and Sudan, who accuse Addis Ababa of unilateral action. Ethiopia insists the filling is “essential for power generation.” Analysts warn renewed disputes could complicate AU mediation efforts.

Source: Al Jazeera

Kenya — Security

Al-Shabab kills five Kenyan security personnel in ambush

Five Kenyan security personnel have been killed while on patrol near the Somalia border in Mandera county by the armed group al-Shabab. According to a Kenyan police report, a Special Operations Group patrol, an elite police “counter-terrorism” unit, came under fire near Wantey Dam, about 6km (4 miles) from Lafey police station, shortly after midday.

Five members of the security forces were killed in the initial assault. A reinforcement team dispatched to the scene was then struck by a roadside bomb that destroyed an armoured vehicle, though no one on board was hurt.

Source: Al Jazeera

Kenya — Energy & Environment

Greenpeace threatens legal action over Dangote Lamu refinery

A $17 billion bet on Kenya's coast. The proposed Dangote refinery for Lamu is projected to produce 700,000 barrels per day, but faces a threatened Greenpeace legal challenge over environmental review.

Greenpeace Africa said it is mulling a potential legal challenge to stop the issuance of approvals for the construction of a multibillion-dollar Dangote Refinery on the Kenyan coast. The government hopes the $17 billion project, which is expected to produce 700,000 barrels-per-day when finished, will create tens of thousands of jobs and boost the region’s energy autonomy.

But it has also drawn ire from activists. Greenpeace argues the Kenyan government made political and financial commitments before undertaking an Environmental and Social Impact Assessment or extensive public participation around the proposed site in Lamu. The plan comes with political weight: Sources close to the Lamu governor said that with national elections coming in August 2027, the administration is keen on the project’s success. The piece of land expected to host the project has already been designated, and Lamu expects to approve various operational licenses required for construction to begin.

Source: Semafor

Kenya — US Health Data Deal

Kenya High Court challenge over US health data deal continues

Kenya’s legal challenge against the US health agreement signed last December, which pledged approximately 1.6 billion dollars over five years with Kenyan contribution of about 850 million dollars, continues after Court of Appeal lifted a suspension in May. A final ruling is due at the end of October. The core deal involves moving Kenyan health data to the US, with disbursement conditional on the data crossing the border, African Business magazine reported.

The Kenya Legal and Ethical Issues Network on HIV and AIDS noted the agreement grants legal immunity to American personnel and contractors, suggesting Kenyan courts have no jurisdiction in data misuse disputes...A separate issue involved a US-built 50-bed isolation facility at Laikipia air base for American personnel exposed to Ebola in DRC and Uganda. Despite local protests and High Court orders, Samaritan’s Purse confirmed seven US staff began a 21-day quarantine there in mid-July. Police killed three people during protests from late May into June.

Source: Xinhua

Kenya — Human Interest

From Athletics Dream to War Captivity: Family Pleads for Son’s Return From Ukraine War

37-year-old athlete Evans Kibet left Kenya on July 27, 2025, in search of a better future and instead became caught up in the Russia-Ukraine war. Evans’ mother, Jane Muneria recalls that Evans informed the family he had secured an opportunity to travel to Russia for athletics after being linked by a friend. For two weeks after his departure, communication suddenly stopped.

Later, the family learnt the shocking truth that the promising athlete had allegedly been deceived into joining the Russian military before eventually being captured by Ukrainian forces. The family has knocked on every door they could think of. They wrote to Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi through his Communications Officer, Jacob Ng’etich, after being advised to formally present their appeal. The family later felt encouraged when Mudavadi publicly mentioned Evans’ case during an interview while on an official visit to Russia. Kipyego has also sought help from Athletics Kenya because Evans was an athlete, but months later, no breakthrough has been communicated.

Source: The Standard

HEALTH ALERT: MADAGASCAR MPOX

Madagascar — Health

Explosive Mpox Outbreak Causes 3,000 Cases in Madagascar

More than 3,000 cases of mpox have been recorded in Madagascar after the virus spread from a single port city to some of the country’s busiest coastal hubs. A total of 3,022 cases and 20 deaths have been recorded as of this week, with cases in Toamasina and Taolagnaro accounting for more than half of all diagnoses. The outbreak has been linked to Clade 1b mpox, a strain that emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024...Scientists believe the virus arrived in the Madagascan port city of Mahajanga via sea trading routes early this year, before spreading through the country’s commercial transport networks to Toamasina and Taolagnaro.

Source: Telegraph

SUDAN: WAR IN ITS FOURTH YEAR

Sudan — Child Soldiers

Child Soldiers Recount Horrors of Sudan’s War and Presence of Colombian Mercenaries

The teenage boy’s hands and legs were shackled to the anti-aircraft gun mounted on a pickup as Sudanese warplanes attacked. He saw another child chained to the steering wheel. As their captors sought cover, the terrified children were ordered to stay and shoot down the jets over the capital, Khartoum. If they tried to flee, they’d be killed by their captors — if the planes didn’t get them first.

The boy, now 17, told The AP that those who ordered him strapped to the gun were Colombian mercenaries providing military aid to Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF) against the army in the war, now in its fourth year. Another child said he was forced to carry out artillery strikes and beaten for disobedience. The rare, firsthand accounts show the perils faced by tens of thousands of children believed to have been conscripted into the war by all sides. Six former child soldiers who were abducted and forced to fight with the Rapid Support Forces, known as the RSF, spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal. Two said they were trained by Colombians.

Source: AP

Sudan — Military

Sudanese army says RSF fighters surrender after gains

A group of Rapid Support Forces fighters surrendered to the Sudanese army with their full military equipment in Omdurman on Friday, state media reported, following what the army described as significant advances this week in North Kordofan state. Military forces said they secured four strategic areas, including Bara and Jabrat al-Sheikh, along with a 400-kilometre trade corridor linking Omdurman to El Obeid.

Former RSF commander Al-Nour al-Qubba, who defected to the army in April, was among officials receiving the surrendering fighters and said desertions from the paramilitary group were continuing. He urged remaining RSF members to lay down arms, saying authorities would accept anyone who stops fighting. The surrender adds to a string of recent defections as the more than two-year-old war grinds through its central Kordofan front.

Source: Sudan Tribune

Sudan — North Kordofan

Retreating RSF Troops Launch Reprisal Attacks on Civilians in North Kordofan

A large contingent of retreating Rapid Support Forces (RSF) launched retaliatory attacks against civilians in North Kordofan. Retreating fighters looted local markets completely, raided residential homes, and arrested scores of residents under accusations of sharing coordinates with the Sudanese military, sources said. The reprisal attacks coincided with a series of drone strikes, presumed to belong to the Sudanese army, targeting RSF convoys in Sodari, Um Badr, and El Mazroub.

… Sodari serves as a vital strategic corridor that the RSF previously used to transport military supplies and fighters between Darfur and Khartoum. The escalation follows the army and its allies regaining control of about five strategic areas in North Kordofan, including the critical export road linking Khartoum to Kordofan and Darfur.

Source: Sudan Tribune

Sudan — Peace Talks

RSF-backed coalition boycotts UN- and AU-led talks in Addis

An alliance of Sudanese political factions aligned with the Rapid Support Forces declined to join a second round of exploratory peace consultations in Addis Ababa on Saturday, citing procedural flaws in how the talks are structured. The Founding Sudan Coalition, known as Tasis, joins the anti-war Somoud coalition led by former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok and the Sudan Liberation Movement of Abdel Wahid al-Nur in boycotting the round.

The consultations are facilitated by a joint mechanism comprising the African Union, United Nations, European Union, Arab League and IGAD, aimed at establishing a civilian-led political transition. Tasis spokesman Ahmed Togod Lisan said the group wants a “comprehensive review” of participant-selection criteria but still supports international mediation and requested direct talks with the mechanism. The rival Democratic Bloc coalition chose to participate in the current round.

Source: Sudan Tribune

Sudan — Humanitarian

Sudan’s conflict continues to reshape regional humanitarian priorities

Displacement without end. Families shelter at a makeshift camp as Sudan's civil war, now in its fourth year, continues to drive one of Africa's largest humanitarian crises.

International humanitarian agencies continue to warn that Sudan’s civil war remains one of Africa’s largest displacement crises, with renewed fighting in several areas complicating relief operations and limiting civilian access to assistance. During the past week, aid organisations reported fresh operational challenges as insecurity affected transport corridors and humanitarian deliveries.

Relief agencies said millions remain dependent on emergency assistance while access negotiations continue with armed actors operating across different parts of the country. While military developments continue to evolve, food insecurity, disrupted health services and disease risks continue to increase in several affected regions.

Source: Al Jazeera

REGIONAL POLITICS

Uganda/Kenya — Politics

Activists in Kenya Demand Release of Ugandan Opposition Leader Kizza Besigye

Activists gathered in Kenya’s capital of Nairobi on Thursday to demand the release of Ugandan opposition leader Kizza Besigye, a day after he collapsed in court in Kampala. The activists described Besigye’s condition as critical and accused Ugandan authorities of frustrating due process in the opposition leader’s treason case.

… They also called for the release of Erias Lukwago, Besigye’s lawyer who is being held in Luzira Prison with charges linked to the case. … Besigye fell in the dock last Wednesday while protesting his trial without lawyers of his own choosing, after authorities detained his main attorney, Erias Lukwago, and charged him with alleged failure to report acts of treason. Besigye’s wife, UNAIDS Executive Director Winnie Byanyima, said in a post on X that Besigye is unconscious in an intensive care unit at a public hospital in the Ugandan capital of Kampala.

Source: Africanews

Uganda — History & Diplomacy

Army chief unveils statue of Israel PM’s brother who died in Entebbe rescue mission

Uganda has unveiled a statue of Yonatan Netanyahu, the older brother of Israel’s prime minister, who was killed during the Entebbe hostage rescue mission 50 years ago. Uganda’s army chief Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba said the monument honoured his courage and selfless service.

Kainerugaba described the mission as “one of the most significant episodes in modern history” and spoke of the now close ties between the two countries as a “remarkable journey”. The statue of Netanyahu, striding forward with a machine gun in his hands, stands outside the old airport terminal where the rescue happened. “May their memories continue to inspire future generations in the pursuit of peace, justice and human dignity,” the army chief said. , 4 hostages, and the hijackers and three accomplices who joined them in Uganda were also killed, as well as at least 45 Ugandan soldiers, in fighting with the Israelis.

Source: BBC

Comoros — Governance

Officials banned from attending weddings during working hours

Comoros said it will ban civil servants from attending weddings during working hours, in a bid to reduce absenteeism among government employees. “Too often, when a citizen goes to an administrative office to obtain a document, they are told that the official has gone to a wedding and they must return the next day,” the interior minister said, adding the change would help public services run better.

Workplace absenteeism amounts to significant inefficiencies: Nine of out the 10 least labor-productive countries in the world last year were in sub-Saharan Africa, according to the International Labour Organization. One Comorian groom-to-be told RFI that his wedding plans wouldn’t be affected “one iota” by the new memo.

Source: RFI

CENTRAL AFRICA

Central African Republic — UN

UN Extends Sanctions against Armed Groups in Central African Republic

The United Nations Security Council on Wednesday unanimously adopted a resolution extending sanctions against armed groups and individuals operating in the Central African Republic. The measures include asset freezes, travel bans, and restrictions on supplying weapons and military equipment to armed groups.

Council members acknowledged Bangui’s gains in democratic governance, security, and state authority. But they warned that armed groups and cross-border arms networks continue to threaten stability, particularly in border regions.

Source: Africanews

Chad — International Justice

Gov’t moves closer to withdrawing from the ICC

Chad has advanced plans to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC), joining a growing debate among several African governments over the court’s role and relationship with the continent. Several governments have previously questioned what they describe as the disproportionate focus of ICC investigations on African conflicts.

Human rights organisations have urged Chad to reconsider, and legal experts note that even if withdrawal proceeds, Chad would remain bound by obligations relating to investigations opened while it was still a State Party unless otherwise determined under the Rome Statute.

Source: Al Jazeera

NORTH AFRICA

Algeria — Transport Safety

Bus plunges into ravine killing at least 27

A passenger bus has crashed into a ravine in northern Algeria, killing at least 27 people and injuring 39 others, according to the country’s health minister. Travelling from the city of Setif to the capital Algiers on Friday, the bus skidded about 50km (30 miles) from its destination and plunged into a deep ravine.

The Civil Protection agency said that the bus had left the road for unknown reasons. “The justice system will crack down with an iron fist and without any leniency once the investigation into the accident has been completed”, said a statement from the authorities. Human factors, including speeding, are the main cause of crashes in the country, according to Algerian road safety authorities. Last year, 3,838 people died, and more than 37,000 were injured in traffic accidents.

Source: Al Jazeera

SECURITY: EGYPT PORT STRIKE

Egypt — Security

LNG Tanker Hit in Damietta Drone Strike

On 30 July, a drone strike targeted the U.S.-owned LNG tanker Energos Winter at Damietta Port, igniting a fire that spread to the sister vessel Gaslog Salem. Egyptian authorities confirmed the incident as the first attack on Egyptian soil since the February Iran-U.S. escalation.

The Port Authority insisted operations remain “fully efficient,” contradicting reports of disruption. Analysts warn the strike signals widening regional conflict spillover into Egypt’s energy infrastructure.

Source: Democracy Now!

Egypt — Security

Egyptian PM Announces Investigation After Damietta Port Drone Attack

Egypt’s Prime Minister said that the country would now be examining the remains of a drone that attacked two vessels at the Egyptian port of Damietta on Wednesday. … On Wednesday, British maritime security firm Ambrey said drone strikes ignited fires on two natural gas vessels at the Egyptian port of Damietta.

It was not immediately clear who was responsible for the strikes on a U.S.-owned floating storage facility and a Greek-owned tanker. No injuries were reported. Egypt, a close U.S. ally and regional mediator, is one of the only countries in the Middle East to have been spared direct military action during the war. A strike by Iran or its allies, if confirmed, would mark a significant widening of the conflict.

Source: Africanews

MIGRATION CRISIS: CEUTA

Morocco/Spain — Ceuta

Ceuta Mass Crossing Sparks Crisis

Largest crossing since 2021. Migrants and Spanish security forces on the beach at Ceuta on 30 July, after an estimated 60,000 people entered the enclave from Moroccan territory in a single mass crossing.

On 30 July, Ceuta saw its largest mass crossing since 2021, with Spanish officials reporting 60,000 migrants entering from Moroccan territory. Moroccan media framed the incident as a sovereignty issue, coinciding with Throne Day celebrations. Algerian outlets accused Rabat of “weaponising migration.” The crisis has reopened sensitive debates on Ceuta and Melilla’s status in Moroccan-Spanish relations.

Source: Euronews

Morocco/Spain — Ceuta

Ceuta migrant rush deaths hit 72 as Spain erects floating barrier

At least 72 migrants died during last week’s mass crossing into Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta, where tens of thousands swam from Morocco, local officials said Sunday. Most of the estimated 60,000 people who rushed into Spain’s North African territory have since returned to Morocco, following the territory’s largest mass migrant crossing.

Spanish police and troops patrolled the streets of Ceuta Sunday as the enclave returned to normal after the sudden mass influx of migrants from Morocco. Only small groups of migrants were still walking around after most who crossed the small border barrier returned voluntarily to Morocco in 48 hours. The largest migrant rush into the enclave has caused an international crisis for Spain, with European partners criticizing Madrid for its immigration policies.

Source: Reuters

Morocco — Diplomacy

Trump says Morocco named a highway after him: Why it matters

The announcement by United States President Donald Trump that Morocco had named an important highway after him came as a surprise to many, not least because Rabat itself has remained silent. In a post on his Truth Social platform on Sunday, Trump thanked Morocco’s monarch, King Mohammed VI, and said he looked forward to travelling on the “Great Highway one day”.

The 1,055km (655.5-mile) highway links southern Morocco with Mauritania and carries a price tag of about $1bn. It runs from Tiznit through Guelmim and Tan-Tan before reaching Laayoune, the main city in Morocco-controlled Western Sahara, a UN-designated non-self-governing territory that Morocco calls its “southern provinces” and where it has invested heavily in roads, ports and other infrastructure over the past two decades. Analysts say those projects are part of a broader effort to strengthen Morocco’s hold over the disputed territory.

Source: Al Jazeera

Tunisia — Economy

IMF Talks Resume Amid Fiscal Strain

Tunisian Finance Minister Fadhel Abdelkefi confirmed resumption of talks with the International Monetary Fund over a stalled $1.9 billion loan. Negotiations had been frozen since April amid political disputes. The government faces mounting fiscal pressure, with July inflation hitting 10.4%. Analysts warn failure to secure IMF support could trigger deeper economic instability.

Source: Reuters

SOUTHERN AFRICA

Angola — Diaspora

Jacinto left Angola for Canada’s Arctic. Now he’s running its only bus service

When a battery tray jammed on one of his buses during a sunny Arctic morning, Jacinto Marques had only minutes to keep Iqaluit’s fledgling public transit service running. He quickly dispatched a backup bus—a repurposed school bus painted black—ensuring commuters could still reach work. Such improvisation defines Marques’ effort to establish public transportation in Iqaluit, Canada’s only Arctic city.

Originally from Angola, the 36-year-old entrepreneur has become owner, mechanic, security guard and problem-solver for Iqaluit Transit, which he launched in March after purchasing used buses from Philadelphia and Edmonton. Marques first came to Iqaluit after befriending an Inuit classmate in Ottawa and later visiting the Arctic. What began as curiosity evolved into a long-term commitment as he recognised both the city’s economic potential and its growing need for public transport.

Home to about 8,300 people, Iqaluit has expanded rapidly since becoming the capital of Nunavut in 1999, attracting government workers and immigrants. Yet residents without cars had long relied on expensive taxis or lengthy walks. Launching the service required ingenuity. Marques and his brother shipped buses north on the annual sealift, modified them with off-the-shelf technology and built a live tracking system.

Winter mornings often begin before dawn, warming engines in sub-zero temperatures. Although ridership has dipped during the warmer months as many Inuit families head out fishing and hunting, Marques remains optimistic. He believes the service will become indispensable as the cold returns, proving that even in Canada’s remote Arctic, reliable public transport is possible through determination and community spirit.

Source: NYTimes

Botswana — Pan-African Cooperation

Boko urges African unity in minerals partnership

President Advocate Duma Boko called for African countries to overcome colonial-era stereotypes and build lasting partnerships during a courtesy call by Côte d’Ivoire’s Minister of Mines, Petroleum and Energy Mamadou Sangafowa Coulibaly at the Office of the President on Wednesday. “It is time for Africa to come together as one, overcome barriers such as distance and language, and build a future founded on unity, cooperation and shared prosperity,” Boko said.

Coulibaly said his delegation was in Botswana to learn from one of the world’s leading mining jurisdictions, particularly interested in Botswana’s experience in managing natural resources and governance frameworks. The engagement demonstrates practical Pan-Africanism, Coulibaly said.

Source: Botswana Daily News

SOUTH AFRICA

South Africa/Nigeria — Diplomacy

Pop star Tyla cancels Lagos concert amid South Africa-Nigeria row over immigration

South African singer-songwriter Tyla has removed a scheduled show in Nigeria as tensions over anti-immigrant violence hamper relations between the two countries. No reason was given for the change to her tour, but it came after some Nigerians on social media had called for a boycott of the show.

For months, South Africa has been the scene of protests - some of them violent - against African immigrants that demonstrators have blamed for crime, unemployment and a strain on public services. Nigeria has become particularly outspoken on the issue, and tension was evident as high-ranking officials from Abuja and Pretoria met this week at the Nigerian ministry of foreign affairs.

Source: TRT Afrika

South Africa — Education

Oprah Winfrey to close her school for girls in South Africa

US talk-show host Oprah Winfrey says the school for girls that she launched in South Africa nearly 20 years ago will close next year. At the end of the 2027 academic year, the expansive boarding school campus near Johannesburg is to be handed over to local education authorities as per the original agreement, her statement says.

Students enrolled at the Oprah Winfrey Leadership Academy for Girls (OWLAG) who will not have graduated when it closes will be offered full scholarships elsewhere. More than 1,000 girls have graduated from the school aimed at those from under-privileged backgrounds and inspired after Winfrey met anti-apartheid icon and former South African President Nelson Mandela in 2002. According to the US star’s Oprah Daily website, many of the school’s graduates have become doctors, lawyers, engineers, artists, executives and entrepreneurs.

Source: BBC

ZAMBIA: ELECTION COUNTDOWN

Zambia — Elections

Final ballot papers land in Zambia as country enters last stretch before August 13 vote

Zambia’s Electoral Commission confirmed Friday that the last consignment of ballot papers for the 13 August general election has arrived in Lusaka, completing delivery of all election materials. The final shipment of 185 pallets landed at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport aboard a chartered Boeing 747 from Dubai, bringing the total to 387 pallets delivered this week.

ECZ chief electoral officer Brown Kasaro received the consignment alongside representatives of political parties and civil society observers. The announcement comes as campaigning intensifies between the ruling United Party for National Development and opposition figures including Patriots for Economic Progress leader Brian Mundubile, with accusations of “manufactured” incidents circulating on both sides in the campaign’s final two weeks.

Source: Lusaka Times

Zimbabwe — Mining & Industry

Zimbabwe gets its first lithium processing plant

China’s Prospect Lithium Zimbabwe opened a $400 million lithium sulfate processing plant, part of efforts by African governments to capture more of the added value in mining industries. The plant, just outside Harare, is now fully operational, months after the government froze the export of raw minerals ahead of a complete ban next year.

“The era of ‘horse and rider’ investment relationships is over,” President Emmerson Mnangagwa said recently. Zimbabwe is Africa’s leading producer of lithium, a key ingredient used to make rechargeable batteries for electric vehicles. PLZ is also planning to open a local lithium carbonate plant, the next point along the processing sequence. Harare has said its ultimate ambition is to make batteries and solar panels domestically; most are currently manufactured in China.

Source: Semafor

Zimbabwe — Politics

A quiet day in Harare after Zimbabwe’s shutdown call

Harare’s streets have been quieter than usual as residents wait to see whether a call for a nationwide shutdown against constitutional changes would lead to protests. The first thing that stood out was the cars on the roads leading into the city centre on Friday were fewer than usual. The morning rush hour that normally fills the capital’s streets was missing…

Across the city, the security presence was difficult to miss. Police blocked access to a popular park where people often gather, making it clear that no one would be allowed inside. In areas where taxis operate and small businesses line the streets, some shops had opened while others remained closed.

Source: Al Jazeera

“The era of ‘horse and rider’ investment relationships is over.”

CAMEROON: LEADERSHIP UNCERTAINTY

Cameroon — Politics

Biya’s Absence Deepens Uncertainty

93 and counting. Cameroonian President Paul Biya, pictured at a public ceremony, has now spent more than 53 days outside the country amid an official blackout on discussing his health.

Cameroonian President Paul Biya has remained outside the country for a record 53 days, renewing questions over the 93-year-old leader’s prolonged stay in Switzerland as government officials and opposition figures offer sharply contrasting accounts. Biya left Cameroon on June 7 for Switzerland with his wife, Chantal Biya, in what government officials described as a private visit.

More than seven weeks later, authorities have yet to say when the president is expected to return. His prolonged absence has fuelled speculation about his health and ability to govern, despite a government ban introduced during a previous extended stay abroad in October 2024 that prohibits public discussion of the president’s health. Government officials, however, maintain that Biya remains in charge of state affairs from Switzerland. Communications Minister René Emmanuel said the president is in good health and continues to work from the European country.

Source: Africa News

Days President Paul Biya, 93, has spent outside Cameroon

Ghana — Agriculture

Forecast of 16 per cent cocoa production fall

Ghana’s cocoa regulator COCOBOD warned of a sharp drop in output next season, expecting a decline of at least 16 per cent. Heavy rains, potential El Niño conditions, and swollen shoot disease have taken a toll, particularly in Western and Western North regions, which produce over half of Ghana’s cocoa. Illegal gold mining has also worsened the crisis as cocoa farms are taken over by miners. Ivory Coast, the world’s largest cocoa producer, is also forecasting a significant drop in output, raising concerns over global supplies.

Source: GhanaWeb

PUBLIC HEALTH: LIBERIA'S KUSH CRISIS

Liberia — Public Health

The kush crisis: The hidden trade behind a generation at risk

Kush, a cheap and highly addictive synthetic street drug, has spread across parts of West Africa and become one of Liberia’s most urgent public concerns. First reported in neighbouring Sierra Leone, it has since spread into Liberia where parents say they have watched young people slip into addiction and struggle to return to everyday life. For families trying to help relatives recover, treatment options remain limited.

Liberia’s government rehabilitation centre in Bentol City, about 30km (19 miles) from Monrovia, remains unfinished. Many families are left to seek help from private facilities, some of which doctors say operate without trained staff or proper oversight…The exact contents of kush remain unclear in Liberia. Authorities know the drug is spreading, but further testing is still needed to determine the substances being mixed into it. Research from other parts of West Africa has found that kush can contain dangerous combinations of synthetic substances, making its effects unpredictable.

Source: Al Jazeera

Approximately 10 Nigerien soldiers were killed in a Boko Haram attack on Friday near a garrison town in Diffa region. The attack occurred in the Lake Chad region, shared by Nigeria, Niger, Chad and Cameroon, where Boko Haram maintains camps. The insurgency, which erupted in 2009, has displaced millions in northeast Nigeria alone and spilled across borders. A regional military coalition to fight jihadist groups suffered setbacks after Niger withdrew following its military takeover.

Nigeria — Crime

Authorities Dismantles Major Meth Cartel

Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) has uncovered the country’s largest industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory in Ogun State. Authorities arrested seven Nigerians and three Mexicans and seized more than 2.4 tons of chemicals as well as crystal meth valued at over $345 million.

The case has intensified concerns that international drug cartels are expanding meth production in Nigeria, with security experts warning of links between organized crime and terrorism in West Africa. Meth seizures and raids on labs in Nigeria have been on the rise since around 2011, according to a 2019 report from the Institute for Security Studies, as Latin American specialists exported their expertise to the country. Florence Banjo, a local farmer, said that the stench from the meth lab would sometimes drift into her nearby village, about a kilometer away. The bust underscores Nigeria’s struggle with transnational crime networks.

Nigeria — Justice

Nigeria is Finally Prosecuting Terrorists at Record Levels. Here’s What That Means

For nearly two decades, Nigeria’s response to Boko Haram, the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) and Ansaru relied largely on military operations, while the justice system lagged behind. Thousands of suspects, many reportedly innocent, spent years in military detention without trial. That is now beginning to change.

Between January and July 2026, Nigeria secured at least 865 terrorism-related convictions, according to the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA). Achieved through the country’s Mass Trial Programme, the figure accounts for more than half of all terrorism convictions recorded since the programme began, according to ONSA Director of Legal Services Zakari Mijinyawa.

Chief of Army Staff Lt. Gen. Waidi Shaibu appointed commanders to four newly established Nigerian Army divisions, following President Bola Tinubu’s approval. The restructuring includes three new brigades, aimed at expanding operational reach against evolving security threats. Analysts view the move as a bid to strengthen command and control amid insurgency challenges.

Source: Naija News

Suspected political thugs attack journalists

About 12 journalists were attacked in Ezza South Local Government Area while travelling to cover an event of a new Peoples Democratic Party member. The journalists, travelling in an official vehicle marked “Correspondents Chapel, Nigeria Union of Journalists,” were reportedly attacked by suspected thugs linked to the ruling All Progressives Congress.

Over 20 armed policemen were at the original venue, a short distance from where the road was blocked.

Presidential aides criticised Cardinal John Onaiyekan for publicly disclosing details of a closed-door 28 July meeting with President Bola Tinubu. The cardinal said the President appeared unhappy, adding “there are so many people hanging around Mr President, giving him a rosy picture.” One presidential aide said the bishops’ assessment “is neither scripture nor an article of faith” and argued there had been measurable improvements in salary and pension payments; another aide accused the Catholic Church of political bias.

US-AFRICA RELATIONS

Continental — US Relations

US to make $20,000 visa deposit requirement for African visitors permanent

The United States has made permanent a visa bond programme requiring citizens from 50 countries—most of them in Africa—to pay a refundable security deposit when applying for business and tourist visas. Under new regulations, the maximum bond has increased from $15,000 to $20,000, while the minimum has risen from $5,000 to $10,000.

Introduced as a pilot programme in August 2025 to curb visa overstays and illegal migration, the bond is refunded if a visa is denied or if the holder complies with the terms of their stay. The U.S. State Department said the programme significantly improved compliance, with visa overstays among affected countries falling from nearly 45,500 in 2024 to fewer than 50 during the pilot’s first ten months. Critics, however, argue the policy unfairly targets applicants from poorer countries, creating financial barriers for family visits, education and business travel.

Source: TRT Afrika

Continental — US Relations

US health aid terms spark sovereignty backlash across Africa

Washington’s new bilateral health agreements face mounting resistance from African nations over provisions requiring citizens’ health data, biometric records, and minerals access. Ghana rejected the deal in April, Zimbabwe walked away in February, and Zambia shelved its agreement in May after demands to open copper, cobalt and lithium industries to American companies.

The agreements generally require African countries to treat FDA approvals as principal bases for approving health products, sidelining national regulators. Kenyan courts have been contesting implementation since December, with a final ruling due in October. More than 50 civil society organisations, including Resilience Action Network Africa, warned leaders the terms serve US strategic goals. Ghanaian officials said the 109 million dollars pledged was contingent on sharing 25 years of health records and real-time integration of biometric databases, bypassing the country’s 2012 Data Protection Act. Cybersecurity experts warned biometric data cannot be reset if compromised.

Source: Xinhua

Continental — Diplomacy Gaffe

US map of Africa mislabels every country at AIDS conference

Every country, mislabelled. A US government map shown at the AIDS 2026 conference in Rio de Janeiro on 30 July 2026 placed Nigeria in the Sahara, Mozambique in the Horn of Africa, and Ivory Coast on the wrong side of the continent.

A US government map displayed at the AIDS 2026 conference in Rio de Janeiro last week mislabeled every African country, causing a stir among attendees. The image showed Nigeria, where the US has several hundred troops deployed, as landlocked in the Sahara Desert. Mozambique appeared in the Horn of Africa, while Ivory Coast was relocated across the continent.

State Department spokesperson said the map was produced by a team member who hastily changed the slide deck before the event and took “full responsibility” for the confusion.

The African Union has approved a broader discussion on migration following calls by Ghana for xenophobic violence in South Africa to receive formal attention within AU structures. Archbishop of Canterbury committed to £100m slavery fund

The Archbishop of Canterbury has renewed her commitment to a controversial £100m fund over the Church of England’s role in the transatlantic slave trade. Dame Sarah Mullally was speaking on a visit to Cape Coast Castle in Ghana where enslaved Africans were held before being trafficked to the Americas.

“We played a part in the transatlantic slave trade. That is clear. Part of the Christian belief in repentance is about action, so we are putting in place action to support those communities that feel the legacy of the slave trade,” she said. The Church of England’s missionary arm ran slave-farmed plantations in the Caribbean to fund the spread of Anglicanism, individual members of clergy were slave owners, and the Church received large donations from slave traders.

Confederation of African Football holds the key to Infantino’s FIFA fate

FIFA president Gianni Infantino’s leadership has become “radioactive” and his 10-year reign as head of world football “is over”, a former head of IOC marketing told AFP. A FIFA plan to raise up to $4.2 billion, based on a valuation of $20 billion, through private investment leaked to media on Tuesday. Following a furious global reaction, Infantino on Saturday shelved the scheme.

Michael Payne, former head of marketing at the International Olympic Committee, noted that: “One week ago, Infantino was riding high from delivering a very successful World Cup, and expected to run unopposed for election next year to continue his mandate as president of FIFA.
